Succeeding John XXIII, this pontiff carried the Second Vatican Council to its 1965 close and built historic bridges with Eastern Orthodox and Protestant churches — who was he?
Pope Paul VI: Head of the Catholic Church from 1963 to 1978.

She served as France's Minister of Justice under Sarkozy before later becoming Minister of Culture across four different governments, and has been mayor of one of Paris's arrondissements since 2008. Who is this French politician?

This short-lived 1990s state in the Balkans seceded from a disintegrating Yugoslavia in 1992, triggering a three-year war as rival Serb and Croat factions carved out their own unrecognized quasi-states — what state?
Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Balkan country (1992–1995)

A vocal critic of the Federal Reserve and mass surveillance programs, this Texas congressman ran for president as the Libertarian nominee in 1988 before seeking the Republican nomination twice more — who is he?

In 1982 this child from Manchester, Maine wrote a letter to Soviet leader Yuri Andropov — and got a personal reply inviting her to visit the USSR, making her 'America's Youngest Ambassador' — who was she?
Samantha Smith: American child peace activist (1972–1985)
Founded in 312 BC by one of Alexander the Great's generals, this Hellenistic Greek state stretched from Anatolia to Afghanistan before Pompey folded it into Rome — which state was it?
Seleucid Empire: Hellenistic state in West Asia (312–63 BC)
Nicknamed "the firebrand," this radical feminist helped found three New York organizations and in 1968 staged a symbolic "Burial of Traditional Womanhood" — who was she?

In July 1995, more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in and around a town the UN had declared a 'safe area' — an event now recognized as the first legally proven genocide in Europe since World War II. What is it called?
Srebrenica massacre: 1995 genocidal killing of Bosniak Muslim men.
In 2007 this French politician became the first woman to reach the second round of a presidential election, ultimately losing to Nicolas Sarkozy — who is she?
Raised by his mother Aethra before discovering his royal father in Athens, this Greek hero is famed for slaying the Minotaur — who is he?
Theseus: Legendary king of Athens who slayed the Minotaur.
Founded by Mamata Banerjee in 1998 as a breakaway faction, this West Bengal party ruled from 2011 until finally losing to the BJP in the 2026 election — which party?
Trinamool Congress: Political party in India.
This Mexican revolutionary-turned-president oversaw the drafting of the 1917 constitution and kept his country neutral in World War I before being assassinated in 1920 — who is he?
Venustiano Carranza: President of Mexico from 1914 to 1920.
Also known by the English name Ivan, this Taiwanese civil and transportation engineer joined the Legislative Yuan in December 2024 — who is he?
Wang Yi-chuan: Taiwanese politician and engineer (born 1972)
This Union general won fame for military strategy but condemnation for the scorched-earth campaigns he waged against the Confederacy — who was he?
William Tecumseh Sherman: United States Army general (1820–1891)
A Tokyo-born artist tied to New York's Fluxus scene, she turned her 1969 honeymoon into a public protest and later recorded in the Plastic Ono Band — who is she?
Yoko Ono: Japanese artist and activist (born 1933)
Which of these people was born first?
Joan Clarke (born 1917) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four. It is particularly useful in handling structured data, i.e., data incorporating relations among entities and variables.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Maria Goeppert Mayer is a physicist. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Which of these is a chemist?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele is a chemist. Carl Wilhelm Scheele (German: [ˈʃeːlə], Swedish: [ˈɧêːlɛ]; 9 December 1742 – 21 May 1786) was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist.
What is the atomic number of Livermorium?
Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
What is the atomic number of Polonium?
Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
In what year was Ferruccio Lamborghini born?
Ferruccio Lamborghini: In 1959, he opened an oil burner factory, Lamborghini Bruciatori, which later entered the business of producing air conditioning equipment.
In what year was Josef Mengele born?
Josef Mengele: Before the war, Mengele received doctorates in anthropology and medicine, and he began a career as a researcher.
In what year did Michael Rockefeller die?
Michael Rockefeller: Michael Clark Rockefeller (May 18, 1938; disappeared November 19, 1961) was an American anthropologist and art collector and member of the Rockefeller family.
In what year did Arthur Schopenhauer die?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 – 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
In what year did Ludwig Wittgenstein die?
Ludwig Wittgenstein: Wittgenstein was born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families.
In what year was Calcium discovered?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
Which company manufactures Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet?
Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet: McDonnell Douglas. The Super Hornet is in service with the armed forces of the United States, Australia, and Kuwait.
Which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15 from?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Soviet Union. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.
Who is credited with discovering Molybdenum?
Molybdenum: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
Who is credited with discovering Serotonin?
Serotonin: Arda Green. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
Who is credited with discovering Beryllium?
Beryllium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
Stretching from the thoracic diaphragm to the pelvic brim, this body region sits between the chest and the pelvis — which body part?
Abdomen (also belly or stomach in vertebrates, or metasoma in arthropods) is the front part of the torso between the thorax (chest) and pelvis in humans and in other vertebrates.

This Austrian psychotherapist founded a school of psychology emphasizing birth order and belonging, breaking from Freud by proposing that contributing to others is key to a person's sense of worth — who is he?
Alfred Adler (Austrian; February 7, 1870 - May 28, 1937) was an Austrian medical doctor, psychotherapist, and founder of the school of individual psychology.
This joint region where the foot meets the leg comprises three joints built from the talus, tibia, and fibula, enabling the foot's up-and-down flexing motions — what body part is it?
Ankle is the area where the foot and the leg meet.
Four novels and fifty-six short stories about a certain consulting detective made his name — but this knighted British writer-physician also invented Professor Challenger. Who was he?
Arthur Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 - 7 July 1930) was a British writer and physician.
Not contagious and believed to be partly genetic, this multi-system inflammatory condition can also cause blood clots, aneurysms, or blindness in severe cases — which condition?
Behçet's disease (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
Born as Hughes Helicopters' Model 77 to replace the AH-1 Cobra, this twin-turboshaft attack helicopter packs a 30 mm chain gun and Hellfire missiles in a tandem cockpit — what is it?
Boeing AH-64 Apache (-) is an American twin-turboshaft attack helicopter with a tailwheel-type landing gear and a tandem cockpit for a crew of two.
This basic unit of digital information most often consists of eight bits, and is called an 'octet' in network protocol documents to avoid ambiguity. What is it?
Byte is a unit of digital information that most commonly consists of eight bits.
Combining science, aesthetics, and technique, this field is the study and practice of making and using maps to communicate spatial information — what field is it?

Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps. The fundamental objectives of traditional cartography are to:

Set the map's agenda and select traits of the object to be mapped.
Besides identifying the laws of elastic collision, this Dutch polymath studied Saturn's rings and improved the design of the telescope — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens (14 April 1629 - 8 July 1695) was a Dutch mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor who is regarded as a key figure in the Scientific Revolution.
Scholars still argue whether it merely transmits meaning or also creates it, but the simplest definition of this concept is the transmission of information — what is it?
Communication is commonly defined as the transmission of information.
Grown from tubers and known by the folk name 'sowbread,' this Primulaceae genus features flowers with distinctively upswept petals — which plant genus?
Cyclamen is a genus of 25 species of perennial flowering plants in the family Primulaceae.
This Russian chemist's great law let him predict three undiscovered elements — germanium, gallium, and scandium — and a synthetic element now bears his name; who was he?
In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, honored for her analysis of how communities govern shared commons — which political economist was she?

Elinor Ostrom (ne Awan; August 7, 1933 - June 12, 2012) was an American political scientist and political economist whose work was associated with New Institutional Economics and the resurgence of political economy.
This ground-nesting songbird of Europe and the Palearctic sings its signature tune while hovering high over farmland and heath, and now also breeds in Australia and Hawaii — what is it?
Eurasian skylark (Alauda arvensis), commonly referred to in Europe as the lark, is a passerine bird in the lark family, Alaudidae.
Madagascar's largest carnivore, this slender, long-tailed mammal evolved cougar-like features independently and climbs trees head-first thanks to flexible ankles — what is it?
Fossa (animal) (Cryptoprocta ferox; FOSS- or) is a slender, long-tailed, cat-like mammal that is endemic to Madagascar.
The largest of four living anteater species, this terrestrial mammal of Central and South America is known for its elongated snout, bushy tail, and long foreclaws. What is it?
Giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
A retrovirus that gradually dismantles the human immune system, it leads to AIDS and, untreated, shortens life by roughly a decade — what is it?
HIV (HIVs) are two species of Lentivirus (a subgroup of retrovirus) that infect humans.
First unearthed in 1994 in Spain's Gran Dolina cave, this Early Pleistocene human was named 'pioneer man' because it was among the first to settle Western Europe. Which species is it?

Homo antecessor (Latin for 'pioneer man') is an extinct species of archaic human recorded in the Spanish Sierra de Atapuerca, a productive archaeological site, from 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago during the Early Pleistocene.
More than 20 types make up this genetic skin condition, whose Greek-derived name means "fish" — a nod to its hallmark dry, thickened, scaly texture — which disorder?
Ichthyosis is a family of genetic skin disorders characterized by dry, thickened, scaly skin.
This billionaire computer programmer co-founded WhatsApp before selling it to Facebook for $19.3 billion in 2014 — who is he?
Jan Koum (born February 24, 1976) is an American billionaire businessman and computer programmer.
Linked to a herpesvirus and immune suppression, this cancer causing purple skin lesions was already being described by Hippocrates in the 300s BC — which condition?
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that can form masses on the skin, in lymph nodes, in the mouth, or in other organs.

Spread by the bite of sandflies and caused by a genus of protozoal parasites, this tropical disease can present as skin ulcers, disfiguring mucosal damage, or a more dangerous internal form. Name the disease?
Leishmaniasis is a wide array of clinical manifestations caused by protozoal parasites of the Trypanosomatida genus Leishmania.
Named for antennae often longer than its own body, this insect family boasts over 35,000 species and gets its name from a Greek myth about a shepherd transformed after angering nymphs — which group?
Longhorn beetle (Cerambycidae), also known as long-horned or longicorns (whose larvae are often referred to as roundheaded borers), are a large family of beetles, with over 35,000 species described.
An autosomal dominant flaw in the fibrillin-making FBN1 gene gives this disorder its tell-tale look — tall, long-limbed, double-jointed — while quietly threatening the aorta — what is it?
Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a multi-systemic genetic disorder that affects the connective tissue.

This chemical compound, typically administered by vein injection, is primarily used to treat methemoglobinemia and was used for over a century against malaria. Common side effects include headache, nausea, and vomiting. What is it?
Methylene blue is a salt used as a dye and as a medication.
Containing antimicrobial lysozymes and immunoglobulins, most of this protective body fluid is produced in the gastrointestinal tract — what is it called?
Mucus is a slippery fluid produced by, and covering, mucous membranes.
Also called niacin, this organic compound is an essential vitamin B3 that plants and animals produce from the amino acid tryptophan. What is it?
Nicotinic acid is an organic compound and a vitamer of vitamin B3, an essential human nutrient.
Many species in this cosmopolitan, often-fragrant family live as epiphytes on trees, and some have ditched leaves entirely — relying on highly specialized pollination tricks instead. What are they?
Orchid are plants that belong to the family Orchidaceae, a diverse and widespread group of flowering plants with blooms that are often colourful and fragrant.

One of the 20th century's most prolific mathematicians, this Hungarian championed Ramsey theory — the study of when order must inevitably appear — and cracked countless open problems across number theory and combinatorics; who was he?
Paul Erdős (26 March 1913 - 20 September 1996) was a Hungarian mathematician known as one of the most prolific mathematicians and producers of mathematical conjectures of the 20th century.
This genus of spiders in the family Ctenidae is found mainly in northern South America, with a single species ranging into Central America — name this genus?
Phoneutria is a genus of spiders in the family Ctenidae.
Born Joseph Ratzinger in Bavaria, this pontiff led the Catholic Church from 2005 until an unusual resignation in 2013, after which he adopted an 'emeritus' title — who was he?
Pope Benedict XVI (born Joseph Alois Ratzinger; 16 April 1927 - 31 December 2022) was the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 2005 until his resignation in 2013.
Nesting in burrows or rock crevices on coastal cliffs, this black-and-white seabird can dive underwater to feed and beats its short wings up to 400 times per minute in flight — what bird is it?
Puffin are any of three species of small alcids (auks) in the bird genus Fratercula.

Covering more than 100 conditions like lupus and Sjögren's syndrome and overlapping heavily with immunology, this branch of medicine tackles inflammation in the joints, muscles and bones — what is it called?

Rheumatology (from Ancient Greek (rhema) 'flowing current') is a branch of medicine devoted to the diagnosis and management of disorders of which the common feature is inflammation in the bones, muscles, joints, and internal organs.

Native to the Azores, Europe, and the Middle East, this tree or shrub's flowers and berries have long been used for cordial and wine, and it also appears in traditional medicine and dietary supplements — name this plant?
Sambucus nigra is a temperate species of tree or shrub in the family Viburnaceae native to the Azores, Europe, and the Middle East.

Though many are crustaceans more closely related to insects than to fish, which group of exoskeleton-bearing aquatic invertebrates, including molluscs and echinoderms, is a leading cause of food allergies?
Shellfish are exoskeleton-bearing aquatic invertebrates used as food, including various species of molluscs, crustaceans, and echinoderms.
This birth defect involves incomplete closure of the spinal column and its surrounding membranes during early pregnancy, occurring in three recognized forms — what condition is it?
Spina bifida (SB; Latin for 'split spine') is a birth defect in which there is incomplete closing of the spine and the membranes around the spinal cord during early development in pregnancy.
Encompassing domestic pigs and their ancestor the Eurasian wild boar, this genus within the even-toed ungulate family Suidae is native across Eurasia and Africa — which genus?

Sus (genus) is the genus of domestic and wild pigs, within the even-toed ungulate family Suidae. Sus includes domestic pigs (Sus domesticus) and their ancestor, the common Eurasian wild boar (Sus scrofa), along with various other species.

Governed by four fundamental laws relating heat, work and temperature to energy and entropy, this branch of physics underpins chemical, mechanical and biochemical engineering alike — which field of physics?
Thermodynamics is a branch of physics that deals with heat, work, and temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and the physical properties of matter and radiation.

Picture a spider that never learned to spin: these extinct arachnids lacked silk-producing spinnerets and wore an abdomen split into three or five distinct plates. Which order, known from the Silurian to the Permian?
Trigonotarbida is a group of extinct arachnids whose fossil record extends from the late Silurian to the early Permian (Pridoli to Sakmarian).
This chronic autoimmune disorder strips patches of skin of their pigment, and in antiquity was often wrongly conflated with leprosy — what is it?
Vitiligo is a chronic autoimmune disorder that causes patches of skin to lose pigment or color; these vary in size and can appear anywhere on the body.

An Iranian-born American surgeon specializing in bariatric and vascular procedures, this reality TV doctor became known for helping morbidly obese patients lose weight on the long-running series My 600-lb Life — name this doctor?
Younan Nowzaradan (born October 11, 1944), also known as Dr.
A pseudoscientific but ancient component of traditional Chinese medicine, this practice involves inserting thin needles into the body, most often for pain relief — what is it called?
Coined in 1852 but now considered stigmatizing in clinical settings, this WHO-estimated 283-million-person global condition involves continued drinking despite the harm it causes — what is it called?
Over 500 of these organic compounds exist in nature, yet only 22 appear in the genetic code, joining together to build proteins — what are they?
Amino acid: Organic compounds containing amine and carboxylic groups.

A German pharmacist coined this pigment's name from the Greek for 'flower' and 'dark blue' in 1835 — it shifts red to purple to blue depending on pH and colors blueberries, black rice, and autumn leaves; what is it?
Native to eastern North America's wet woods and swamps, this shrub genus produces bitter 'chokeberries' that reached Scandinavia and Russia by the eighteenth century — what genus is this?

Aronia: Genus of plants (chokeberries). Aronia is a genus of deciduous shrubs, the chokeberries, in the family Rosaceae native to eastern North America and most commonly found in wet woods and swamps.
Derived from a Greek word meaning 'that which is thought worthy,' which term denotes a statement accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning?
Axiom: Statement that is taken to be true.
This common, noncancerous enlargement of a male gland can cause frequent urination and a weak stream; it isn't linked to poor hygiene, and there's no known cure. What's the condition?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Noncancerous increase in size of the prostate gland.
This small, fluid-filled pocket that forms in the skin's upper layers — usually from friction, burns, or infection — gets the name 'bleb' when it's especially tiny. What is it?
Blister: Small pocket of fluid within the upper layers of the skin. The word "blister" entered English in the 14th century.
Typically about two-thirds copper and one-third zinc, which prehistoric substitutional alloy differs from bronze, which swaps in tin instead of zinc?
Brass: Alloy of copper and zinc. Brass has long been popular for its bright, golden appearance and is used for drawer pulls and doorknobs.
This silvery-gold alkali metal has a melting point just above room temperature, making it one of only five elemental metals that go liquid in warm conditions — what is it?
Caesium: Chemical element with atomic number 55 (Cs)
This Cornell astronomer worked on the Mariner, Viking, and Voyager missions and won a Pulitzer for 'The Dragons of Eden' — who is this famed science communicator?
Carl Sagan: American scientist and science communicator (1934–1996)
Known commonly as tapeworms, this class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed segments called proglottids — what is this class called?
Cestoda: Class of flatworms. Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes).
Known for an exceptionally loud song produced by rapid buckling of drum-like tymbals, some periodical members of this insect superfamily emerge en masse only every 13 or 17 years — which insect?
Cicada: Superfamily of insects. The cicadas are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).
Also known as ubiquinone, this antioxidant cofactor helps mitochondria produce ATP and gets its name from ten isoprenyl units in its molecular tail — what is it?
Coenzyme Q10: Biochemical cofactor and antioxidant. Coenzyme Q (CoQ), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring biochemical cofactor (coenzyme) and an antioxidant produced by the human body.
A heart disease involving reduced blood flow to cardiac muscle due to buildup of plaque in heart arteries — the most common cardiovascular disease. What is it?
Coronary artery disease: Reduction of blood flow to the heart. Procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) may be used in severe disease.
This closed sac in the body, distinct from an abscess of pus, forms a shell of abnormal cells and may contain air, fluid, or semi-solid material — what is it, medically?
Cyst: Closed sac growth on the body. A cyst is a closed sac in the body, having a distinct envelope and division compared with the nearby tissue.

Found in many cough and cold medicines, this morphinan-class compound was approved by the FDA in 2022 as part of a rapid-acting antidepressant combo, but can act as a dissociative hallucinogen at high doses. What substance is it?
Dextromethorphan: Cough suppressant and dissociative drug.
Sold over the counter as Unisom and combined with vitamin B6 to ease morning sickness, this first-generation antihistamine is one of the world's most widely used sleep aids — which drug?
Doxylamine: First-generation antihistamine used as a short-term sedative and hypnotic (sleep aid)
Despite its name, this South American freshwater fish is actually a knifefish, not a true eel, and produces powerful discharges using specialized tissue — which species?
Electrophorus electricus: South American electric fish. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.
This flowering shrub in the family Erythroxylaceae is one of only two species whose leaves are cultivated to produce a notorious stimulant — which plant is it?
Erythroxylum coca: Species of flowering plant.
Sporting an orange-red breast rimmed in grey and brown upperparts, this small insect-eating songbird ranges from Western Siberia to North Africa — which bird?
European robin: Species of bird. It is found across Europe, as far east as Western Siberia, and as far south as North Africa.

This branch of Islamic scholarship interprets the Quran and sunnah through jurist reasoning, producing fatwas — while sharia itself is seen as unchanging, this human field is considered fallible. What is it called?
Fiqh: Islamic jurisprudence. Thus, whereas sharia is considered immutable and infallible by Muslims, fiqh is considered fallible and changeable.

Making up roughly 88% of all living amphibians, this short-bodied, tailless order gets its name from Ancient Greek for 'without tail' — and its warty-skinned members are casually dubbed toads. What is it?
Frog: Order of amphibians. The eggs then hatch into fully aquatic larvae called tadpoles, which have tails and internal gills.
Also known as cranesbills for their pointed seed pods, this 422-species genus bears five-petaled, often veined flowers and includes at least one protocarnivorous species — what's the genus?
A U.S. Navy rear admiral who helped develop COBOL, this computer science pioneer wrote what's considered the first computer manual and worked on the Harvard Mark I — who is she?
Grace Hopper: U.S. naval officer and computer scientist (1906–1992)

Coined by psychologist Edward Thorndike, this cognitive bias describes how a positive impression in one area, like someone's looks, skews our judgment of them in unrelated areas — what is this bias called?
Halo effect: Tendency for positive impressions to contaminate other evaluations.

Synthesized from the dried latex of the opium poppy, this opioid is used medically in some countries to relieve pain during childbirth or a heart attack — and its 'black tar' form is a crude, variable mix of morphine derivatives — what is it?
Heroin: Opioid analgesic and recreational drug.
The flowers of this shrub genus act as natural pH indicators, turning blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil?
Powered by four underperforming Lyulka turbojets, this aircraft became the first Soviet jet bomber to fly before being cancelled in September 1947 — which plane?
Ilyushin Il-22: 1947 Soviet bomber aircraft prototype. The Ilyushin Il-22, USAF/DOD designation Type 10, was the first Soviet jet-engined bomber to fly.
As president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995, this French politician spearheaded the creation of the single market and laid the groundwork for the euro — who is he?
A real estate magnate and Spanish–American War officer worth roughly $87 million, he was the richest passenger aboard the Titanic — and went down with it in 1912. Who was he?
John Jacob Astor IV: American businessman and Titanic passenger (1864–1912)
This German-Finnish internet entrepreneur founded the file-hosting service Megaupload before U.S. authorities seized it in 2012 — who is he?
The last member of the actinide series, this synthetic element honors the man who invented the cyclotron — the very machine used to discover so many artificial elements. Which element is it?
Lawrencium: Chemical element with atomic number 103 (Lr)
Named in honor of a pioneer of sterile surgery, this genus of bacteria causes a rare but serious foodborne illness with a fatality rate up to 30 percent — what is it?
Listeria: Genus of bacteria. Listeria is a genus of bacteria that acts as an intracellular parasite in mammals.
Named from a Greek root meaning 'light' or 'brightness' in reference to its luminous, reflective eyes, this genus includes the bobcat among its four wild cat species — which genus?
Lynx: Genus of medium-sized wild cats.
A Russian pediatric endocrinologist also known by the surname Faassen, this woman is the elder child of Russia's president. Who is she?
Maria Vorontsova: Daughter of Vladimir Putin (born 1985)
Also called pennyroyal, this minty flowering plant native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East has a folk-remedy history despite being toxic to the liver — what species is it?
This twin-engine Soviet fighter, known to NATO as 'Fulcrum,' was built in the 1970s to counter American jets like the F-15 and F-16 — which aircraft is it?
Mikoyan MiG-29: Soviet twin-engine jet fighter aircraft. The Mikoyan MiG-29 (Russian: Микоян МиГ-29; NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.

First identified from skulls found in a Dutch chalk quarry near Maastricht and initially mistaken for crocodile or whale bones, this giant marine lizard genus lived until 66 million years ago — which genus is it?
Mosasaurus: Extinct genus of marine lizard from the Late Cretaceous.
Colloquially known as a moon, this type of astronomical body orbits a planet or dwarf planet, with 455 confirmed examples across the Solar System's six major systems — what is it called?
Natural satellite: Astronomical body that orbits a planet. Natural satellites are colloquially referred to as moons, by analogy with the Moon, Earth's natural satellite.
A catecholamine whose very name nods to the kidney, it acts as both a hormone and neurotransmitter and is called "noradrenaline" outside the US — what is it?
Norepinephrine: Catecholamine hormone and neurotransmitter. The general function of norepinephrine is to mobilize the brain and body for action.
Discovered by naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859, this fungus hijacks carpenter ants' brains and marches them down to the forest floor before killing them — which organism?

Ophiocordyceps unilateralis: Species of fungus. Ophiocordyceps unilateralis, commonly known as zombie-ant fungus, is an insect-pathogenic fungus, discovered by the British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859.
First domesticated in Mesoamerica and led in production today by India, this tropical fruit belongs to the small genus Carica — what is it?
Papaya: Species of tropical fruit plant.
This term describes a short chain of amino acids joined by a particular kind of bond; string together enough of them (10,000 daltons or more) and you get a protein instead — what is it?
Peptide: Short chains of 2–50 amino acids.
Cultivated since the days of the Inca Empire and known in English as the Cape gooseberry or goldenberry, this South American nightshade now grows wild worldwide — which species is it?
Physalis peruviana: Species of cultivated South American fruit. Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru.
Most commonly referring to a type called PET, this category of polymers built from ester linkages is often blended with cotton to reduce wrinkling — what is it called?
Polyester: Category of polymers, in which the monomers are joined together by ester links.
This Old World tree species has two main cultivar groups, the dark-red Morello and the lighter Amarelle, prized for their tart, edible pulp — which fruit-bearing plant?
Prunus cerasus: Species of cherry tree. Prunus cerasus (sour cherry, tart cherry, or dwarf cherry) is an Old World species of Prunus in the subgenus Cerasus (cherries).
A small herbivore of the family Leporidae and a cousin to hares, this prey animal has been introduced to every continent except Antarctica — what is it?
Rabbit: Mammals of the family Leporidae. The most widespread rabbit genera are Oryctolagus and Sylvilagus.
One of the largest land megafauna left, this odd-toed ungulate has five surviving species — two in Africa, three across South and Southeast Asia — and a name meaning "nose-horned." What is it?
Co-founder and first president of Mattel, she dreamed up a certain doll in 1959 and was later portrayed in the 2023 Barbie film — who was she?
Ruth Handler: American business magnate and inventor (1916–2002)
Named from Greek words for 'thorn' and 'earthworm,' which genus of large tropical centipedes gives its name to an entire family of segmented, many-legged predators?
Despite historians noting that email already existed in the early 1970s, this MIT-trained engineer holds a 1982 copyright and claims to have invented it as a teenager — who is he?
Shiva Ayyadurai: American engineer, conspiracy theorist, and entrepreneur.
Raised in the Bronx by Puerto Rican-born parents after her father's early death, this Princeton and Yale Law graduate became the third woman ever named to the U.S. Supreme Court — who is she?
Sonia Sotomayor: US Supreme Court justice since 2009.
Nicknamed 'Woz,' this engineer co-founded a now-giant computer company in 1976 and was the primary designer of the Apple II — who is he?
Steve Wozniak: American engineer and programmer (born 1950)
This Polish tax advisor turned politician placed third in the 2025 presidential election while chairing the libertarian New Hope party — who is he?
Sławomir Mentzen: Polish economist and politician (born 1986)
